editorial.title: Star ratings get gamed. Source documents don't.
editorial.p1: TrustGive aggregates public registries — IRS Form 990, UK Charity Commission, Минюст СОНКО — and links directly to the source documents. We don't publish a trust score. We don't process payments. The job of the platform is to take you to the original record in one click.

about.title: About
about.lead: TrustGive is built and run by one person. It takes no money from charities, runs no ads, and has no investors. Here is who I am and what that means for what you're reading.
about.whoBody: I'm Alex Diachenko. I build software, and I live in Moscow. TrustGive started as a weekend question and turned into the thing I work on. There is no team behind it — when this site is wrong, it's my mistake, and when it's fixed, I fixed it.
about.whyBody1: I went to donate and stopped at a question I couldn't answer: who decides which charities are real? The large rating sites publish scores whose method I couldn't follow, and which nonprofits learn to work around — Charity Navigator dropped its overhead-ratio metric in 2023 for that reason. The donation platforms add 10–18% on top of a gift before the charity sees it.
about.whyBody2: So this site doesn't score anything. It finds the filing the regulator holds and links straight to it. You read the document and decide. Donations happen on the charity's own site, not here.
about.moneyBody: It isn't. Infrastructure costs about nothing — a small database, a worker, free public APIs. Charities cannot pay to be listed, to rank higher, or to be removed. There is no revenue to protect, which is the only reason I can afford to delist an organisation the moment its filing stops resolving.
about.limitsBody: Three limits worth knowing before you rely on anything here:
about.limit1: A verified badge means the organisation is registered and has filed. It says nothing about whether the money is spent well. That's a harder question and I don't answer it.
about.limit2: Coverage follows the registers, not the sector. Countries whose regulators publish machine-readable records are represented; countries whose regulators don't are missing, regardless of how good their charities are.
about.limit3: Filings run one to two years behind. That's the regulator's cycle, not a gap in the data.
about.errorBody: Tell me. I've already found four organisations listed under another entity's registration number — one of them filed under the Gates Foundation. I found those by auditing my own data, but I won't catch everything. A specific report with the charity's name gets fixed faster than a general complaint.
about.openBody: The code, the method and the API are public. You don't have to take my word for how verification works — you can read the code that does it, or query the same data directly.

guides.lead: How to check a charity yourself, using the same public registers this catalogue uses. Every guide is anchored in something we got wrong here first — the mistakes are more instructive than the advice.
guides.footnote: These guides describe registers that change. If something here no longer matches what a register does, that is a mistake worth telling us about: hello@trustgive.org.

what-501c3-status-actually-means.title: What 501(c)(3) status actually means
what-501c3-status-actually-means.standfirst: A line in the US tax code, not a seal of approval. What an organisation had to do to get it, what it is worth to you as a donor, and the four things people reliably assume it proves when it does not.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.intro1: People say "501(c)(3)" when they mean "real charity". The shorthand works often enough to stick around and fails often enough to cause trouble. What the term actually names is a subsection of the Internal Revenue Code, the one the IRS grants federal tax exemption under. Whatever the status tells you comes from that. Nothing else comes from it at all.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.intro2: The blurring tends to happen at the worst possible moment, when somebody is deciding whether to give. What follows is what the status demands, what it hands you, and the point where it runs out.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s1Title: What the organisation had to satisfy
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s1p1: The status goes to organisations "organized and operated exclusively" for one of the exempt purposes the section names: charitable, religious, educational, scientific, literary, testing for public safety, fostering national or international amateur sports competition, and preventing cruelty to children or animals. Purpose aside, three conditions do most of the work.

s1list.0: No private benefit. The IRS puts it this way: "none of its earnings may inure to any private shareholder or individual". Making a surplus is fine. Handing it to insiders is not.
s1list.1: No political campaigning. On intervening in a campaign for or against a candidate, the IRS calls Section 501(c)(3) organisations "absolutely prohibited". Lobbying on issues is allowed, within limits.
s1list.2: Annual reporting to the IRS. Almost always on a form in the 990 series.

what-501c3-status-actually-means.s1p2: That is the entire test. What it leaves out is worth reading twice. Competence is not in there. Results are not in there. Neither is any measure of how much of a donation reaches the work.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s2p1: Every 501(c)(3) sits in one of two categories. The category changes what the organisation has to do, and it changes what you can deduct.

s2list.0: A public charity is supported by the general public, by government, or by other public charities. Churches, hospitals, universities and the ordinary donation-funded organisations most people picture.
s2list.1: A private foundation usually has one source of money behind it, often a family or a company, and tends to make grants instead of running programmes. Stricter rules apply to it, along with an excise tax on investment income.

what-501c3-status-actually-means.s2p2: For a donor the difference that bites is the deduction limit. Gifts to public charities can be deducted against a higher share of your income than gifts to private foundations. Both categories are public, and the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search will tell you which one you are looking at.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s3Title: What it means for your donation
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s3p1: For a US taxpayer who itemises, a contribution to a 501(c)(3) is generally tax-deductible. That is the benefit most people are really asking after when they check the status, and it is genuine.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s3p2: It is narrower than it sounds, though. How much you can deduct depends on the organisation's category, on anything you got back in return, and on your own tax position. Limits vary enough that the IRS assigns deductibility status codes, and its search tool shows the code for every organisation.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s3caution: None of that says anything about quality. Deductibility describes your tax return. A well-run charity and a badly run one are equally deductible.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s4Title: The status can be taken away, quietly
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s4p1: Here is the part that catches people out, because nothing announces it. Miss the required annual return three consecutive years running and the exemption goes automatically. There is no hearing, and donors are not told. An automatically revoked organisation, in the IRS's words, "is not eligible to receive tax-deductible contributions".

s4list.0: The loss is public and checkable. The IRS publishes the Automatic Revocation of Exemption list.
s4list.1: Reinstatement can be applied for, and sometimes granted retroactively, so a name on that list is not automatically a dead organisation.
s4list.2: The website, the brochures and the donation page will usually carry on as though nothing happened.

what-501c3-status-actually-means.s4p2: So the question worth asking is not whether they ever held 501(c)(3) status. It is whether they hold it today.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s5p1: It does not mean effectiveness, or efficiency, or that anyone has ever looked at the results. Less obviously, it does not mean the organisation has filed anything you can actually read. Status and filing are two separate facts, and an organisation can hold the first while still owing the second.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s5case: Four US charities in this catalogue carried a verified badge on tax-exempt status alone, with nothing filed behind it: the national Salvation Army office, Catholic Relief Services, Catholic Charities USA and Founders Pledge. Two of them had no filings of any kind on ProPublica, and the other two had filings that contained no data. Every one resolves, returns the right legal name, and opens when you click it. What opens is a registry record rather than a return. All four were unpublished.
what-501c3-status-actually-means.s6p1: Four steps. None of them costs anything.

s6steps.0: Find the organisation's EIN, the nine-digit employer identification number, on its own website or on a donation receipt.
s6steps.1: Run it through the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search. Check that the name matches, and read the deductibility code.
s6steps.2: Check the Automatic Revocation list in the same tool, or look for a revocation posting date, so you know the status is current and not historical.
s6steps.3: Open the most recent Form 990 and confirm it exists and carries figures. A return with no financial data in it tells you almost nothing.

0.q: Is a 501(c)(3) the same as a nonprofit?
0.a: No. "Nonprofit" is a corporate form granted at state level, while 501(c)(3) is a federal tax status. A body can be incorporated as a nonprofit and never obtain 501(c)(3) status, or hold it and lose it later. Different governments grant them, for different reasons.

1.q: What is the difference between 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(4)?
1.a: Both are tax-exempt, but only gifts to a 501(c)(3) are generally deductible for the donor. A 501(c)(4) social welfare organisation is free to campaign politically in ways a 501(c)(3) is not. Some groups run one of each under similar names, which confuses people constantly.

2.q: Does 501(c)(3) status mean the charity is well run?
2.a: No. The status examines purpose and structure, never performance. Nothing in the application or in the annual return asks whether the work achieves anything.

3.q: The charity is not in the IRS search tool. Is it fake?
3.a: Not necessarily. Churches do not have to apply for recognition, very small organisations may file nothing but the electronic postcard, and the tool's data is refreshed periodically rather than live. Absence is a reason to ask a question, not a verdict.

4.q: How current is any of this?
4.a: Less current than you would expect. The IRS publishes on a lag, and Form 990 data describes a fiscal year that has usually been over for some time. Across this catalogue, the median age of the newest available filing is 31 months.

what-charity-registration-actually-prove.title: What charity registration actually proves
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.standfirst: Hardly anyone wants to know whether an organisation is registered. What they want to know is whether their money will be stolen, and whether it will do any good. Registration answers a third question that nobody asked.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.intro1: You search, the word "registered" comes back at you, and it sounds like the answer to both worries. It is answering something else entirely.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s1p1: Strictly speaking, registration carries two pieces of information. The organisation met the legal test for charitable status wherever it is based, and it now has to file. Nothing else follows from it. What you are looking at is a fact about paperwork.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s1p2: The test itself also differs from place to place. England and Wales have the Charity Commission, Scotland has OSCR, Northern Ireland has CCNI. In the United States, federal status comes from the IRS, while charity registration is handled separately by almost every state. So an organisation that is absent from whichever register you happened to search may be perfectly genuine.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s2p1: It says nothing about effectiveness or honesty, and nothing about whether the organisation still exists. People miss that last one most often. Registers go on serving pages for charities that have shut down. The name is right, the income figure sits where it always did, and a single word of status is all that moves.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s2case: The Big Issue Foundation came off the register on 15 September 2023, and Companies House dissolved the company on 19 December 2023. Its register page opens to this day, and looks entirely healthy.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s3Title: Why I built the catalogue around it anyway
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s3p1: I originally wanted to donate to charities helping children in Africa, and then caught myself thinking: will the money actually go where it should? I started looking for any information about various charities and realised that finding it by hand is hard. So I decided to build a site where you can open the regulator's document for each charity and check it yourself.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s4Title: Why it is still worth checking
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s4p1: What registration does clear away is the bottom layer of fraud, the invented organisations and the people passing themselves off as a well-known charity. Not much, but unlike ratings of effectiveness you can actually check it. Even that minimum turns out to be harder than it sounds.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s4case: Three national registers, the Canadian CRA, the Australian ABR and New Zealand's Charities Services, will hand back an ordinary page with a 200 status for an identifier we made up. Any check that stops at "the link opened" sails through all three. It caught us five times in a row, in different countries.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s5p1: The catalogue started with 541 organisations, but during the manual check I realised that not all of them have proper financial reporting — and the site was presented as a system of verified charities. I was offered the chance to pour in thousands more from ProPublica, and I turned it down: that would have meant publishing records nobody had checked.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s6p1: There are several reasons. The main one is how complicated registration and paperwork are. The other is plain security: TrustGive is my personal project, and with a money-transfer system in place I cannot guarantee your funds will arrive — situations vary, and that would cost the site its credibility.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s7Title: What we check and what we do not
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s7p1: There is one rule here. A record goes live only when the regulator's document opens and names the same organisation. An identifier that merely resolves proves nothing.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s7p2: The database holds 537 records, and 394 of them are published. The remaining 143 wait, and they come back the day someone can confirm them. Canada accounts for 28 organisations and not one is published, because the CRA register offers no stable public address for a record. We say exactly that on the Data Sources page.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s7p3: We do not check effectiveness, the quality of governance, or the share that goes on administration, and we do not attempt to. There is one more thing almost nobody says out loud: freshness. Across the catalogue, the median age of the filings we can reach is 31 months. Six organisations out of 394 have a filing under twelve months old.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s8Title: Why we publish our own mistakes
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s8p1: I think this kind of information helps users understand that this site is about the truth first. I was not trying to build an ordinary project for show: it is a service where a person can check a charity themselves before sending anything. It also shows that getting this wrong is easy. We got it wrong ourselves, even though checking is our whole job.
what-charity-registration-actually-prove.s9p1: A user should know what we checked and what we did not look at. And if a charity is not on the list, that says nothing about it yet: most often we simply could not find a document that opens.

how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.title: How to check if a charity is legitimate
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.standfirst: Six checks, in the order that catches the most problems soonest. None of them requires paying for anything, and the first four take about ten minutes.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.intro1: Almost every guide to this question tells you to look the charity up in an official register. That advice is correct and it is not enough, because it stops one step short of the part that actually goes wrong. A register entry can open, load cleanly, and describe a completely different organisation from the one asking you for money.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.intro2: We know because we did it. This catalogue publishes charities only when a regulator's document opens and names the same organisation, and we still shipped five entries that failed that test. What follows is the checklist we now use, written around the specific ways it can fail.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s1p1: If you only have ten minutes, do these in order and stop at the first one that fails.

s1steps.0: Find the charity's registration number on the charity's own website, not from a search result or an email. In the United Kingdom a registered charity is required by law to state it; in the United States you want the EIN.
s1steps.1: Type that number into the regulator's own register — the Charity Commission, the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search, the ACNC, whichever applies.
s1steps.2: Read the name the register gives back. It must be the organisation you are looking at, not merely something similar.
s1steps.3: Read the status. "Registered" and "Removed" are both real answers, and only one of them means what you want.
s1steps.4: Open the most recent filing or annual return and check it exists and covers a period that has actually ended.

how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s1p2: The rest of this guide is about why each of those steps is worded the way it is, because every one of them replaced a shorter version that let something through.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s2Title: A page that loads is not evidence
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s2p1: The most common mistake is treating "the link worked" as confirmation. It isn't. Several national charity registers return a normal, healthy page for an identifier that does not exist at all — no error, no warning, just a page.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s2case: We tested fabricated identifiers against three national registers. All three answered with HTTP 200 — the code that means "here is the page you asked for" — for numbers we had invented. Any check that stops at "did the page load" would have passed all three. This is why every automated check in this catalogue now reads the content of the page and ignores the status code entirely.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s2p2: For you, as a reader, the practical form of this rule is simple: do not accept a link as proof. Open it and read the organisation's name off the page.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s3Title: The number can belong to someone else
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s3p1: An identifier is not a name. It is a key into a database, and a wrong key returns a real record about a real organisation — which is exactly what makes it convincing. A wrong number does not look broken. It looks fine.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s3case: We published Cure Leukaemia against Charity Commission number 1100994 for months. That number belongs to PAG (Parent Action Group) Limited, a charity removed from the register in 2011. The link opened, the page was real, the number resolved — and it was about a different organisation that no longer existed. Cure Leukaemia's actual number is 1100154.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s3p2: So the check is not "does the number resolve". The check is "does the register, when given this number, name this organisation". Compare the whole name, not part of it: an entry that shares two words out of four is not a match.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s4Title: Registered once is not registered now
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s4p1: Registers keep serving pages for charities that have closed. The record does not disappear — it changes status, often in a single word that is easy to read past when you are looking for reassurance.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s4case: The Big Issue Foundation was removed from the Charity Commission's register on 15 September 2023, and its company was dissolved at Companies House on 19 December 2023. Its register page still opens, still carries the right name, still shows an income figure. Everything about it looks right except the status, and the organisation it describes is no longer a registered charity.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s5Title: You may be looking in the wrong register
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s5p1: Countries with more than one charity regulator are a reliable source of confusion. A charity absent from the register you are searching may be perfectly legitimate and registered somewhere else.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s5case: We had Maggie's stored against an England-and-Wales number, 1058460, which the Charity Commission answers with Euro Charity Trust — a different organisation entirely. Maggie's is a Scottish charity, registered with OSCR as SC024414, and its own website says so plainly. We were searching the wrong regulator and accepted the first number that came back.

s5list.0: United Kingdom: England and Wales (Charity Commission), Scotland (OSCR, numbers beginning SC), Northern Ireland (CCNI, numbers beginning NIC).
s5list.1: United States: the IRS for federal tax-exempt status, plus a separate charity registration in most states.
s5list.2: Canada: the CRA maintains the list of registered charities.
s5list.3: Australia: the ACNC register, with the ABN as the identifier.
s5list.4: New Zealand: Charities Services, numbers beginning CC.

how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s6p1: Register search boxes are usually fuzzy: they match on words, they return neighbours, and they paginate. The organisation you asked about may not be the first result, or on the first page at all.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s6case: Searching the Charity Commission for 219099 — the RSPCA — returns dozens of local RSPCA branches sorted ahead of the RSPCA itself. Our own code asked for that number, read the first page of results, did not find it there, and concluded the register held no such charity. It holds it. The row was simply further down.
how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s6p2: When you search, confirm the number on the result you open matches the number you typed. If it does not, you are reading about a different organisation, however similar the name.

s7list.0: The organisation cannot or will not give you a registration number.
s7list.1: The number it gives resolves to a different name in the register.
s7list.2: The register says the registration has been removed, revoked, or is under investigation.
s7list.3: The donation page is on a domain unrelated to the charity's own, and nothing on the charity's own site links to it.
s7list.4: Pressure to give immediately — a deadline, a matching offer expiring tonight, a caller who will not let you check and call back.
s7list.5: No filings at all, in a jurisdiction where filing is required for an organisation of that size.

how-to-check-if-a-charity-is-legitimate.s7caution: None of these is proof of fraud on its own. Small charities file late, websites are built badly, and a legitimate organisation can look disorganised. Treat them as reasons to check further, not as verdicts.

0.q: Does being registered mean a charity is well run?
0.a: No. Registration means an organisation met the legal test for charitable status and files what it is required to file. It is a statement about paperwork, not about whether the money achieves anything. A registered charity can be ineffective, and an effective organisation can be unregistered.

1.q: The register shows a filing from two years ago. Is that a red flag?
1.a: Usually not. Regulators publish on a lag, and the figure you can see today typically describes a financial year that ended one to three years ago. That is normal almost everywhere. A gap of five years or more is worth asking about.

2.q: What if the charity is not in any register I can find?
2.a: That is a question, not an answer. Small organisations fall below registration thresholds, some countries have no central register, and religious and educational bodies are often exempt. Ask the organisation directly which register it is on and under what name.

3.q: Is a charity's own website good enough evidence?
3.a: For finding the registration number, yes — in several countries stating it is a legal requirement. For confirming the number is real, no. Use the site to learn what to look up, then look it up in the register.

4.q: Someone contacted me claiming to be a well-known charity. How do I check?
4.a: Do not use any link, phone number or address they gave you. Search for the charity independently, go to its own website, and use the contact details published there. Impersonation of real charities is more common than invented ones, because the real name survives the first check.

research.lead: Findings from auditing this catalogue. Published because they hold outside it: anyone assembling charity data from public registers runs into the same walls, and most of them are invisible until you hit one.
research.footnote: Every figure published here is reproducible from the script and the public API linked in each piece. If you find a number that doesn't hold up, hello@trustgive.org.

how-old-is-charity-financial-data.title: Nobody can tell you what a charity spent last year
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.standfirst: Across 365 organisations whose filings we could open, not one has financial information covering a period that ended within the last twelve months. Not one. The median is two and a half years old, and that is the system working as designed.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s1p1: For each of {{measured}} published organisations we took the most recent filing anyone can currently obtain, and asked how long ago the fiscal period it describes came to an end.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s1p2: That is a narrower question than “how slow is the regulator”, and deliberately so. We don't store the date a return was received or published, so we can't speak to regulator speed. What we can measure is what a reader gets when they go looking today — which is the question a donor actually has.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s2Title: The freshest thing available is two and a half years old
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s2p1: The median filing describes a period that ended {{median}} months ago. {{older}} of {{measured}} — 94% — describe a period more than two years gone. The top row of the table is the one worth sitting with.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s2p2: Zero. Not a small number: none. Whatever a donor is told about how a charity spends money, nobody — not this site, not any rating service, not the regulator's own website — can currently show them a filing about the year that just ended.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s3Title: It is a sawtooth, not a delay
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s3p1: The filing dates cluster hard, because fiscal years end on a handful of dates and everything downstream follows:
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s3p2: A charity closes its books on 31 December, has months to file, the regulator processes and publishes, and a mirror picks it up. Each step is reasonable; stacked, they put two and a half years between the money being spent and anyone outside being able to read about it. The lag isn't negligence, and it isn't going to be fixed by anyone shouting at a charity.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s4Title: Countries differ, but far less than you'd expect
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s4p1: Median age of the freshest available filing, by country:
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s4p2: Six months separates the fastest from the slowest — nothing like the coverage gaps in the companion piece, where the same countries range from 100% to zero. The spread within a country tells you more: UK filings sit in a tight band of {{gbMin}} to {{gbMax}} months, because one regulator publishes on one cycle, while the US stretches to {{usMax}} months at the far end, where an organisation's most recent machine-readable return is years behind.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s5p1: “Verified” and “current” are different claims, and only the first one is available. A revenue figure on this site — or on any site built from public filings — describes a year that ended long before you read it. That is worth knowing before treating it as a picture of a charity today.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s5p2: It also sets a ceiling on what charity data can do. Any question of the form “is this organisation in trouble right now” cannot be answered from filings, by anyone, and a service that implies otherwise is selling the appearance of currency rather than the thing.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.method: Measured {{date}} across the {{measured}} published organisations carrying a filing date; 4 more carry none. The figure is the age of the fiscal period the filing covers (ProPublica's `tax_prd`, or the equivalent period end for other registers), not the date the return was submitted or published. Buckets are exclusive; percentages are of the 365 measured.

what-we-could-not-verify.title: A third of the charities we assembled could not be verified — and it was almost never their fault
what-we-could-not-verify.standfirst: 541 organisations went in. 369 came out with a regulator document you can open. The 172 that didn't cluster by country, not by charity, and the reason is what the regulator publishes — not what the organisation does.
what-we-could-not-verify.s1p1: We assembled {{assembled}} organisations from public registers and tried to link each one to a document its own regulator published — a filing, a register entry, something a reader can open and check. {{verified}} of them made it.
what-we-could-not-verify.s1p2: The other {{unverified}} are not published. They stay in the database, and they reappear the moment a document can be found for them, but a directory whose claim is “every entry links to the regulator's own file” cannot carry entries that don't.
what-we-could-not-verify.s2Title: The failure is not broken links
what-we-could-not-verify.s2p1: This is the part that surprised us. Of the {{unverified}} unverified organisations, {{noDocument}} had no obtainable document at all — not a dead link, an absent one. Exactly {{deadLink}} had a document whose link stopped resolving.
what-we-could-not-verify.s2p2: So the common mental model — records rot, links die, catalogues decay — describes almost none of this. The records were never obtainable in the first place. That distinction matters, because the two problems have different fixes: rot needs monitoring, absence needs a different source.
what-we-could-not-verify.s3p1: Sorting the same 541 records by country makes the pattern obvious. The verification rate has almost nothing to do with the organisations and almost everything to do with whether their regulator publishes a stable, per-organisation record that a machine can fetch and a human can read.
what-we-could-not-verify.s3p2: The United Kingdom is at 100% because the Charity Commission gives every registered charity a permanent page keyed to its registration number. The United States is at 87% because the IRS releases Form 990 data that ProPublica mirrors with a stable URL per organisation. At the other end sit countries whose registers exist but are search-only: you can look an organisation up by hand, but there is no address to link to, so there is nothing to show a reader.
what-we-could-not-verify.s4Title: Canada, and a check that would have lied
what-we-could-not-verify.s4p1: Canada is the sharpest case: {{tested}} organisations assembled, none published. It is also where we caught our own worst near-miss.
what-we-could-not-verify.s4p2: The first verification routine written for Canada accepted a registration number if the CRA's charity page returned HTTP 200. Tested against controls, that page returns 200 for a fabricated number — byte-for-byte the same 55,230-byte response as for a real one. Had that routine run, it would have stamped “verified” on every Canadian record including the invented controls. It was disabled before it ever ran.
what-we-could-not-verify.s4p3: Checking the same numbers against a CRA endpoint that returns data rather than a status code gave a different answer: {{genuine}} of {{tested}} resolved to the right organisation, {{wrongEntity}} resolved to a different organisation entirely — one of them to a local parish rather than the national body whose name we had stored — and {{unresolvable}} did not resolve at all. A government-issued identifier that renders on a page is not evidence that it belongs to the organisation next to it.
what-we-could-not-verify.s5Title: What this means if you use charity data
what-we-could-not-verify.s5p1: Two things worth carrying away. First, coverage of any charity directory reflects regulator publishing practice, not sector quality — so an organisation's absence from a directory says far less than its presence. Second, if you are building verification of your own, never accept an HTTP status as proof; require a response that names the organisation, and compare that name to the one you hold.
what-we-could-not-verify.s5p2: We publish only what survives that test, which is why this catalogue is smaller than the data we hold. The gap is the finding.
what-we-could-not-verify.method: Figures measured {{date}} across all records in the database, published and unpublished. “Verified” means at least one source document whose URL returned HTTP 200 at audit time and whose registry record names the organisation. The Canadian identifier testing, including the fabricated controls, is recorded in the project's data-integrity audit.

api.title: Public API
api.lead: The whole catalogue is available as JSON. No key, no account, nothing to sign up for — the endpoints this site runs on are the ones you can query.
api.accessBody: Read-only and anonymous. Responses carry cache headers and are served from the edge, so repeated requests are cheap for both of us.
api.rateLimitValue: 60 requests per minute per IP address
api.endpointsBody: Every endpoint below is a GET and needs no headers.

endpoint.list: Paginated catalogue with filters — the main entry point.
endpoint.detail: One organisation in full: financials, source documents, press mentions.
endpoint.documents: Just the source documents held for one organisation.
endpoint.featured: The homepage selection, plus the real catalogue total.
endpoint.hubs: Country, cause and registry sections with their counts.
endpoint.stats: Catalogue size, countries covered, and when it was last re-checked.
endpoint.causes: The cause taxonomy, in English and Russian.
endpoint.seo: The question-and-verdict payload behind the “Is X a legitimate charity?” pages.

api.exampleBody: Look an organisation up by name or registration number:
api.termsBody: The compilation — which organisations are listed, the identifier held for each, and the document each one links to — is released under CC0 1.0, into the public domain. Take it, republish it, build on it, no attribution required. The filings themselves are a separate matter: TrustGive claims no licence over them, so if you intend to redistribute the documents, the terms are the register's, and each register states its own.
api.termsLink: Which registers the data comes from
api.schemaBody: The OpenAPI 3.1 schema is generated from the code on every deploy, so it can't drift from what the API actually does. Point a client generator at it, or read it in the browser.

search.label: Search charities by name or registration number
search.placeholder: Search by name or registration number
search.noMatchBody: That may mean the organisation is real but we couldn't confirm its regulator filing — unconfirmed organisations aren't published here. Check the spelling, try the registration number, or read how verification works.

sources.title: Data sources
sources.lead: Everything in the catalogue comes from a public register. This page lists which ones, what each covers, and where each falls short.
sources.howBody: A nightly job re-reads every US filing from ProPublica and re-checks every source link in the catalogue. A charity whose link stops resolving is removed from public view the same night — not flagged, removed. Nothing here is entered by hand except the two-sentence descriptions and the translations.

propublica.name: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer
propublica.meta: United States · Form 990 · free, no key
propublica.body: Mirrors the IRS release of Form 990 filings for US 501(c)(3) organisations. Supplies the registration number, the fiscal period covered, total revenue and executive compensation. This is the largest single source in the catalogue.
propublica.limit: Filings appear one to two years after the fiscal year ends, and the API returns nothing for organisations that file on paper or fall below the electronic filing threshold.

charityCommission.name: Charity Commission for England and Wales
charityCommission.body: The statutory register of charities in England and Wales, with accounts and annual returns filed against each registration number.
charityCommission.limit: Covers England and Wales only. Scottish and Northern Irish charities sit under separate regulators that are not yet integrated here.

acnc.name: Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
acnc.body: The national charity register, matched to the Australian Business Register record for each organisation.
acnc.limit: The register does not expose per-charity revenue, so Australian entries carry a verified registration without a money breakdown. Several national bodies share a domain with their state branches, which makes automatic matching unreliable — those are resolved by hand or left out.

minjust.name: Минюст СОНКО
minjust.body: The Ministry of Justice register of socially oriented non-profit organisations, used for the small curated Russian selection.
minjust.limit: Registration confirms legal existence and nothing else. Russian entries are curated rather than loaded in bulk, and the legal exclusions described in the methodology apply.

sources.missingBody: Coverage follows what regulators publish, not what matters. Two absences are worth naming:
sources.missingCanada: Canada. The CRA charity register has no stable public address for an individual charity — the URL that looks like one returns an identical page for every input, including invented registration numbers, and an error in a browser. There is no document to link to, so no Canadian charity is published here.
sources.missingEurope: Most of continental Europe. Charity registers are national and heterogeneous; many publish no machine-readable per-organisation record, and smaller organisations file only on paper.
sources.useBody: The same records the site reads are available from the public API, unauthenticated. If you are citing the catalogue in research, query it directly rather than scraping the pages — and note the date, because entries are removed when their evidence stops resolving.

methodology.title: How we verify
methodology.lead: We don't grade charities. We show you the documents that grade them for us — and link straight to those documents.
methodology.verifiedMeansBody: A charity is marked Verified on TrustGive if all three are true: (1) it is registered with at least one government registry; (2) it has filed financial documents in the last 24 months; (3) we link directly to those documents on the charity's page.
methodology.catalogueTitle: Why this catalogue is smaller than it could be
methodology.catalogueBody: Every organisation listed here has a regulator filing you can open in one click. If we cannot confirm that document, the organisation does not appear at all — we don't publish it with a caveat, a lower rating, or an "unverified" label. A directory that mixes confirmed and unconfirmed entries quietly transfers the checking work back to you, which defeats the purpose.
methodology.catalogueBody2: This has a cost we'd rather state than hide: real, reputable charities are missing from these pages. Some national registers publish no per-organisation record we can link to, and some organisations file only on paper. Their absence is a limitation of what we can prove, not a judgement about them. If a charity you trust isn't here, that is the most likely reason.
methodology.doNotVerifyBody: We do not assess program effectiveness, mission outcomes, or donor satisfaction. For deeper rigor, we recommend GiveWell, Effektiv-Spenden, and CharityWatch.
methodology.complianceBody: TrustGive is operated from Russia. Russian law requires us to exclude the following categories of organisations from our catalogue, regardless of the work they do:
methodology.complianceItem1: Organisations recognised as foreign agents by the Ministry of Justice of the Russian Federation
methodology.complianceItem2: Organisations recognised as extremist or undesirable by Russian courts or executive bodies
methodology.complianceItem3: Organisations providing material assistance to parties of active armed conflicts
methodology.complianceItem4: Organisations registered in territories where compliance with Russian regulations cannot be reliably verified
methodology.complianceFooter: These exclusions are a legal compliance requirement, not an editorial judgement about the work these organisations do. Donors who wish to support such organisations can do so directly through other discovery tools.
methodology.deeperBody: For mission-effectiveness analysis, we recommend GiveWell, Effektiv-Spenden, and CharityWatch.

common.errorBody: This is on us, not on the charity. Please try again in a moment.

drawer.previewUnavailable: Government registries don't allow embedded preview. Open the original to read the full filing.
drawer.notEdited: This is the original filing. TrustGive did not edit it.
drawer.howItWorks: TrustGive links straight to the registry — we don't host or modify charity filings.
